# Region based spatial transcriptomics analysis with scider

## Introduction

`scider` is a user-friendly R package providing functions to model the
global density of cells in a slide of spatial transcriptomics data. All
functions in the package are built on the `SpatialExperiment` object,
allowing integration into various spatial transcriptomics-related
packages from Bioconductor. After modelling density, `scider` supports
several downstream analyses, including colocalization analysis, boundary
detection and differential density analysis.

The plotting functions return `ggplot` objects, so figures can be
further customised with any `ggplot2` layer.

This vignette walks through a typical workflow on a Xenium breast cancer
dataset.

## Load Package

``` r

library(scider)
library(SpatialExperiment)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Load Example Data

The example dataset is a small `SpatialExperiment` object (one Xenium
breast cancer section) hosted as a GitHub Release asset. Download it
once and cache locally:

``` r

data_url   <- "https://github.com/ChenLaboratory/example_data/releases/download/v1.0.0/spe_xenium_bc_s1rep1.rds"
cache_dir  <- tools::R_user_dir("scider", "cache")
data_file  <- file.path(cache_dir, "spe_xenium_bc_s1rep1.rds")

if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  download.file(data_url, data_file, mode = "wb")
}

spe <- readRDS(data_file)
spe
#> class: SpatialExperiment 
#> dim: 313 163797 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(313): ABCC11 ACTA2 ... ZEB2 ZNF562
#> rowData names(3): ID Symbol Type
#> colnames(163797): cell_1 cell_2 ... cell_167779 cell_167780
#> colData names(12): cell_id transcript_counts ... gene_counts cell_type
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):
#> spatialCoords names(2) : x_centroid y_centroid
#> imgData names(1): sample_id
```

## Data exploration

The Xenium data was annotated by 10X Genomics. The cell type annotation
is summarized below.

``` r

table(colData(spe)$cell_type)
#> 
#>           Stromal    Invasive_Tumor              DCIS       Macrophages            Myoepi       Endothelial      CD4+_T_Cells      CD8+_T_Cells            Others           B_Cells 
#>             41422             38149             24604             12798              9938              8931              8453              6940              5769              4987 
#> Perivascular-Like               DCs        Mast_Cells 
#>               847               792               167
```

We can visualize the spatial distribution of all the cell types across
the tissue as follows.

``` r

plotSpatial(spe, group.by = "cell_type")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Or visualize the spatial distribution of specific cell types (e.g., DCIS
and Invasive Tumor).

``` r

COI <- c("DCIS", "Invasive_Tumor")
sel <- spe$cell_type %in% COI
plotSpatial(spe[, sel], group.by = "cell_type")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

We can also examine the expression level of each individual gene
spatially. Because the returned object is a `ggplot`, we can add a title
with [`ggtitle()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/labs.html).

``` r

plotSpatial(spe, feature = "FOXA1", type = "log") +
  ggtitle("FOXA1 expression (log-scale)")
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Cell type density

`scider` implements grid-based density analysis for spatial
transcriptomics data. We first calculate density for each cell type
using function `gridDensity`. The calculated density and grid
information are saved in the `metadata` of the `SpatialExperiment`
object. The size of the grid (bin) is set by the `grid.length.x`
parameter, and the level of smoothing is set by `bandwidth`.

``` r

spe <- gridDensity(spe, grid.length.x = 50, bandwidth = 50)
```

We can visualise the overall (all cell types) density of the whole
tissue using function `plotDensity`. The `probs` parameter indicates the
density percentile below which the grids are filtered (not plotted).
Setting `probs` to 0 will plot everything including the background.

``` r

plotDensity(spe, probs = 0)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Alternatively, user can specify `cutoff` to filter grids with low cell
density. The density values represent the expected numbers of cells at
each grid.

``` r

plotDensity(spe, cutoff = 5)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

We can also visualise the density of specific cell type(s).

``` r

plotDensity(spe, coi = COI)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Find Regions-of-interest (ROIs)

After obtaining grid-based density for each cell type, we can then
detect regions-of-interest (ROIs) based on density of certain cell
type(s). This is done by using the `findROI` function.

Here we identify ROIs based on the cell density of DCIS and invasive
tumor. The `min.density` parameter filters grids with low cell density,
whereas the `ngrid.min` gives the minimum number of grids that each ROI
should have.

``` r

spe <- findROI(spe, coi = COI, min.density = 0.5, ngrid.min = 20)
#> Overwriting the probs argument. Grids are filtered by the min.density value.
```

The ROIs can then be visualized using `plotROI`.

``` r

plotROI(spe, roi = COI)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Testing relationship between cell types

After defining ROIs, we can test whether the densities of any two cell
types are spatially correlated, within each ROI or overall while
accounting for ROI variation. This is done with function `corDensity`.
By default it compares the observed correlation between two cell type
densities with the correlations obtained under random labelling: cell
locations are kept, cell type labels are shuffled and the densities are
recomputed (999 times by default). Because the p-values come from these
random relabellings, we set a seed for reproducible results. The
modified t-test of Dutilleul, which accounts for the spatial
autocorrelation between neighbouring grids, is available with
`method = "modified.ttest"`.

``` r

set.seed(1)
results <- corDensity(spe, roi = COI)
```

We can examine the correlation between each pair of cell types in each
ROI. Besides the observed correlation (`cor.coef`), the results give its
expected value under random labelling (`cor.expected`), the difference
between the two (`shift`), and one-sided p-values for positive (`p.Pos`)
and negative (`p.Neg`) association.

``` r

results$ROI
#> DataFrame with 3276 rows and 9 columns
#>        celltype1      celltype2         ROI     ngrid   cor.coef cor.expected      shift     p.Pos     p.Neg
#>      <character>    <character> <character> <integer>  <numeric>    <numeric>  <numeric> <numeric> <numeric>
#> 1        Stromal Invasive tumor           1       202 -0.0774348     0.613646  -0.691081         1     0.001
#> 2        Stromal Invasive tumor           2       128 -0.6751916     0.732848  -1.408039         1     0.001
#> 3        Stromal Invasive tumor           3       248 -0.8019436     0.825980  -1.627924         1     0.001
#> 4        Stromal Invasive tumor           4       171 -0.8022129     0.778160  -1.580373         1     0.001
#> 5        Stromal Invasive tumor           5       227 -0.6857148     0.769038  -1.454753         1     0.001
#> ...          ...            ...         ...       ...        ...          ...        ...       ...       ...
#> 3272        D cs     Mast cells          38        54         NA  0.055113517         NA        NA        NA
#> 3273        D cs     Mast cells          39       108 -0.0571595  0.015804798 -0.0729643 0.5844422  0.416581
#> 3274        D cs     Mast cells          40       132  0.1020318  0.010188023  0.0918438 0.3750000  0.626000
#> 3275        D cs     Mast cells          41       103  0.6772782 -0.000472391  0.6777506 0.0111675  0.989848
#> 3276        D cs     Mast cells          42        62         NA  0.093383468         NA        NA        NA
```

Or the correlation between each pair of cell types across all ROIs. The
overall results also count the ROIs in which the observed correlation
lies above (`n.above`) or below (`n.below`) its expected value, or is
significantly so (`n.sig.Pos`, `n.sig.Neg`):

``` r

results$overall
#> DataFrame with 78 rows and 12 columns
#>             celltype1      celltype2   cor.coef cor.expected      shift     p.Pos     p.Neg     n.roi   n.above   n.below n.sig.Pos n.sig.Neg
#>           <character>    <character>  <numeric>    <numeric>  <numeric> <numeric> <numeric> <integer> <integer> <integer> <integer> <integer>
#> 1             Stromal Invasive tumor -0.5021193     0.678683 -1.1808023     1.000     0.001        41         0        41         0        41
#> 2             Stromal           Dcis -0.2910660     0.632843 -0.9239088     1.000     0.001        40         1        39         0        39
#> 3             Stromal    Macrophages  0.2575724     0.550896 -0.2933232     1.000     0.001        42         8        34         3        20
#> 4             Stromal         Myoepi  0.0541824     0.514875 -0.4606926     1.000     0.001        40         1        39         0        33
#> 5             Stromal    Endothelial  0.5209102     0.499207  0.0217035     0.132     0.869        42        17        25         8         8
#> ...               ...            ...        ...          ...        ...       ...       ...       ...       ...       ...       ...       ...
#> 74            B cells           D cs   0.318719    0.1409202  0.1777986     0.001     1.000        40        31         9        13         2
#> 75            B cells     Mast cells   0.261348    0.0776230  0.1837254     0.001     1.000        39        26        13         7         1
#> 76  Perivascular like           D cs   0.175935    0.0770501  0.0988851     0.001     1.000        40        26        14         7         0
#> 77  Perivascular like     Mast cells   0.132619    0.0473268  0.0852918     0.014     0.987        39        24        15         5         1
#> 78               D cs     Mast cells   0.164990    0.0449535  0.1200369     0.001     1.000        38        22        16         7         3
```

We can visualise the statistics between each pair of cell types using
function `plotCorHeatmap`. Two cell type densities tend to rise and fall
together with the local number of cells, so the observed correlations
are mostly positive. The `shift` measures co-localization (positive) or
segregation (negative) beyond this, and is easier to interpret. Here we
show the shift in each ROI for a selection of cell types:

``` r

plotCorHeatmap(results, level = "ROI", stats = "shift",
               cell.type = c("DCIS", "Invasive_Tumor", "Stromal",
                             "Macrophages", "CD8+_T_Cells", "B_Cells"),
               fontsize_col = 6)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Or the shift for all cell type pairs across the whole slide:

``` r

plotCorHeatmap(results, stats = "shift", fontsize_row = 8, fontsize_col = 8)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Accounting for tissue compartments

The strongest results above are between tumour cells and the surrounding
cells, which largely reflects the separation of the tumour from the rest
of the tissue. To look for structure beyond such compartments,
`corDensity` can shuffle the cell type labels only among cells of the
same compartment, given by a column of `colData` passed to
`permute.within`. The arrangement explained by the compartments then
becomes part of the expected value.

Here we group the cell types into epithelial, stromal and immune
compartments. Cells annotated as `Others` are placed in the stromal
compartment. Compartments should be coarse: a cell type that is the only
type in its compartment is never shuffled.

``` r

compartment <- c(DCIS = "epithelial", Invasive_Tumor = "epithelial",
                 Myoepi = "epithelial",
                 Stromal = "stromal", Endothelial = "stromal",
                 `Perivascular-Like` = "stromal", Others = "stromal",
                 Macrophages = "immune", `CD4+_T_Cells` = "immune",
                 `CD8+_T_Cells` = "immune", B_Cells = "immune",
                 DCs = "immune", Mast_Cells = "immune")
spe$compartment <- unname(compartment[spe$cell_type])
table(spe$compartment)
#> 
#> epithelial     immune    stromal 
#>     104175      19502      40120
```

``` r

set.seed(1)
results_within <- corDensity(spe, roi = COI, permute.within = "compartment")
```

For two cell types in the same compartment, a positive shift now means
that they share neighbourhoods more than two random cells of that
compartment would. For cell types in different compartments, it means
that they lie closer to each other than random cells of their
compartments would. The pairs with the largest shifts are:

``` r

res <- as.data.frame(results_within$overall)
res <- res[order(abs(res$shift), decreasing = TRUE),
           c("celltype1", "celltype2", "cor.coef", "cor.expected", "shift",
             "n.sig.Pos", "n.sig.Neg")]
res[3:5] <- round(res[3:5], 2)
print(head(res, 12), row.names = FALSE)
#>       celltype1      celltype2 cor.coef cor.expected shift n.sig.Pos n.sig.Neg
#>         Stromal Invasive tumor    -0.50         0.85 -1.35         0        37
#>         Stromal           Dcis    -0.29         0.81 -1.10         0        40
#>         Stromal        B cells     0.57        -0.27  0.85        30         3
#>         Stromal    Endothelial     0.52        -0.20  0.72        29         1
#>         Stromal    Cd8 t cells     0.42        -0.29  0.71        33         2
#>  Invasive tumor           Dcis     0.12         0.81 -0.69         2        32
#>          Myoepi    Endothelial     0.05         0.70 -0.65         0        38
#>     Macrophages         Myoepi     0.08         0.73 -0.65         0        39
#>         Stromal    Cd4 t cells     0.44        -0.20  0.64        28         3
#>          Myoepi    Cd4 t cells     0.09         0.69 -0.60         0        36
#>            Dcis         Myoepi     0.37        -0.19  0.56        35         0
#>         Stromal         Others     0.25        -0.28  0.53        25         1
```

Within the epithelium, DCIS cells co-localize with myoepithelial cells
and segregate from invasive tumour cells, consistent with the
myoepithelial layer that surrounds ducts in DCIS but is lost in invasive
carcinoma. The fibroblast-like stromal cells lie further from tumour
cells, and closer to B and T cells, than random cells of the respective
compartments would.

## Cell density contour

Another strategy to partition a tissue spatially is to construct cell
density contours. This can be done using the `getContour` function.

The `equal.cell` parameter ensures roughly equal cell numbers across all
density levels.

``` r

spe <- getContour(spe, coi = COI, equal.cell = TRUE)
#> Finding contour using total density of input COIs.
#> Using bins = 10 to draw contours with equal cell numbers.
```

The constructed contours can be visualised using `plotContour`.

``` r

plotContour(spe, coi = COI)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)
